title: Sarah laughs (Genesis 18:9–15)
hookLine: told she will bear a child at ninety, she laughs; the child will be Isaac, "he laughs"
last: HACHNASAT ORCHIM — RUN TO THE GUEST.

lines: A SON, THIS TIME NEXT YEAR.
cards: The three strangers have eaten. Then one of them asks a question guests don't usually ask: where is Sarah, your wife? In the tent, Abraham says.
And the guest says: I'll come back this time next year, and Sarah your wife will have a son. Sarah is standing just inside the tent door, listening. She's about ninety.
Abraham is nearly a hundred. The Torah says, with real frankness, that the time for her to bear children had long passed.
So she does what anyone would do, hearing a stranger say something that absurd about their own body. She laughs. Not out loud.

teach.b: What she says inside is honest and a little funny: after I'm worn out, am I going to have pleasure, and my husband is old too?
Then God speaks to Abraham: why did Sarah laugh, saying, shall I really bear a child, now that I'm old? Listen closely. Sarah said, my husband is old.
God reports her as saying, I am old. The rabbis caught this, and loved it.

teach.h: GOD CHANGES HER WORDS FOR PEACE.
teach.b: The Talmud says God changed her words for the sake of peace in the home, so Abraham wouldn't be hurt. Great is peace, they said: even God shades a sentence to keep it.
Then comes the question at the heart of the story: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" Sarah gets scared and denies it. I didn't laugh.
The answer comes back, almost gently: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." Not a punishment. Just: you did.
And it's not only Sarah. A chapter earlier, when God first promised this son, Abraham fell on his face and laughed too. Both parents laughed.
So when the baby comes, a year later, Abraham gives him the name God had already chosen: Yitzchak, Isaac. It means he laughs, or he will laugh. The name keeps the joke forever.

teach.h: GOD HATH MADE LAUGHTER FOR ME.
teach.b: And Sarah, holding him, says: "God hath made laughter for me." Everyone who hears, she says, will laugh with me. Her laugh starts as disbelief and ends as joy, and it's the same laugh.

how: Jews read Sarah's laughter in the Torah portion Vayera, and the rabbis' teaching that God changed her words for the sake of peace is often cited as a lesson about protecting peace at home.

o: her laugh of disbelief that turned into joy
a polite laugh to welcome the strangers
a laugh that mocked God and was punished

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: only Sarah laughed at the promise of a son
Abraham laughed first, a chapter earlier, falling on his face.
God repeated Sarah's words exactly to Abraham
she said my husband is old; God said she'd said I am old. the Talmud says it was for peace.
the name Isaac means he laughs
Yitzchak, from the Hebrew root for laughter.

games.q: you're Sarah, about ninety. God has just asked why you laughed, and you're scared. what do you say?
games.why: she denies it, afraid, and the answer is gentle and plain: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." a year later her son is named he laughs.

practice: Think of one thing that seems impossible to you right now: getting well, making up with someone, finishing the degree, changing a habit that's older than your kids.
Say it to yourself plainly, and let yourself smile at it, even laugh a little, the way Sarah did behind the tent: not mocking, just honest that it seems absurd.
Hold the laugh and the hope side by side, and if you pray, you can offer both.

wordCard.voice: Sarah laughs. Disbelief behind a tent door that turned into joy, and a son named Isaac, he laughs.

orig.note: Hebrew: Isaac, he laughs or he will laugh.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing is too hard. Even a laugh can become a name. Day forty-four, done.
